\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{index::doc}}


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{Fair Language Processing} (FairLangProc) package is an extensible open\sphinxhyphen{}source Python library
containing techniques developed by the research community to help detect and mitigate bias in
Natural Language Processing throughout the AI application lifecycle.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The FairLangProc package includes:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Datasets} \sphinxhyphen{} Benchmarks to test for biases in NLP models

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Metrics} \sphinxhyphen{} Fairness measures based on different philosophies to quantify bias

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Algorithms} \sphinxhyphen{} Bias mitigation techniques at pre\sphinxhyphen{}processing, in\sphinxhyphen{}processing, and intra\sphinxhyphen{}processing stages

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
It has been created with the intention of encouraging the use of bias mitigation strategies
in the NLP community, with the hope of democratizing these tools for the ever\sphinxhyphen{}increasing set
of NLP practitioners.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{tip}{Tip:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The companion paper provides a comprehensive introduction to the concepts and capabilities,
with all code available in the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/arturo-perez-peralta/FairLangProc/tree/main/notebooks}{notebooks}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you use this library in your research, please cite our \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03677}{arXiv paper}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxstepscope


\chapter{Getting Started}
\label{\detokenize{getting_started:getting-started}}\label{\detokenize{getting_started::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This chapter provides an introduction to FairLangProc, including installation,
quick start examples, and a comparison with other fairness tools.


\section{Why FairLangProc?}
\label{\detokenize{getting_started:why-fairlangproc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A unified framework for fairness in NLP with comprehensive coverage of datasets, metrics, and algorithms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are several tools available for bias mitigation in the fair ML landscape:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{AI Fairness 360 (aif360)} \sphinxhyphen{} The main inspiration for this project. Provides bias mitigation methods for tabular data but lacks NLP\sphinxhyphen{}specific features.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Fairlearn} \sphinxhyphen{} Offers fairness tools but is not focused on NLP.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{AllenNLP} \sphinxhyphen{} Provides embedding metrics and debiasing methods but development has been discontinued.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Dbias} \sphinxhyphen{} Offers a pipeline for bias evaluation but uses a custom methodology.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{LangFair} \sphinxhyphen{} Allows generating custom datasets for fairness evaluation but lacks debiasing algorithms.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{langtest} \sphinxhyphen{} Comprehensive evaluation library but with limited bias mitigation capabilities.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
FairLangProc addresses these limitations by providing:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{NLP\sphinxhyphen{}First Design} \sphinxhyphen{} Specifically designed for text data with HuggingFace transformers integration

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Comprehensive Coverage} \sphinxhyphen{} 13+ benchmark datasets, 8+ fairness metrics, and 9+ debiasing algorithms

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Pre/In/Intra\sphinxhyphen{}Processing} \sphinxhyphen{} Support for all stages of the ML pipeline

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Unified Interface} \sphinxhyphen{} Consistent API across all modules

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Active Development}

\end{itemize}

\chapter{Metrics}
\label{\detokenize{metrics:metrics}}\label{\detokenize{metrics::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
FairLangProc provides comprehensive fairness metrics to measure discrimination in NLP models.


\section{Supported Metrics}
\label{\detokenize{metrics:supported-metrics}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
FairLangProc supports different fairness metrics to measure discrimination in NLP. Broadly, they can be classified into three categories:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Embedding metrics} (WEAT, SEAT): if they measure bias by examining the model’s hidden representations of input text.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Probability metrics} (LPBS, CBS, CPS, AUL): if they measure bias by computing the probabilities of certain tokens or sentences.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Generated text metrics} (DR, SA, HONEST): if they measure bias by examining text generated by the model, looking for harmful or stereotypical words.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The implemented metrics are:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{xref}{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Generalized association tests (WEAT)}}} \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.07187}{(Caliskan et al., 2016)}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{metrics:metric-lpbs}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Log Probability Bias Score (LPBS)}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.07337}{(Kurita et al., 2019)}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{metrics:metric-cbs}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Categorical Bias Score (CBS)}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.42/}{(Ahn et al., 2021)}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{metrics:metric-cps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{CrowS\sphinxhyphen{}Pairs Score (CPS)}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://aclanthology.org/2020.emnlp-main.154/}{(Nangia et al., 2020)}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{metrics:metric-aul}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{All Unmasked Score (AUL)}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.07496}{(Kaneko et al., 2021)}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{metrics:metric-dr}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Demographic Representation (DR)}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.09110}{(Liang et al., 2022)}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{metrics:metric-sa}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Stereotypical Association (SA)}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.09110}{(Liang et al., 2022)}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{metrics:metric-honest}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{HONEST}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://aclanthology.org/2021.naacl-main.191/}{(Nozza et al., 2021)}.

\end{itemize}


\section{Embedding Metrics}
\label{\detokenize{metrics:embedding-metrics}}

\subsection{WEAT}
\label{\detokenize{metrics:weat}}\label{\detokenize{metrics:id2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The most famous embedding metric is given the Word Embedding Association Test (WEAT) \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.07187}{(Caliskan et al., 2016)},
which aims to measure associations between demographic and neutral attributes. Demographic attributes are usually binary and denoted by \(A_1, A_2\),
denoting two different societal groups (male and female, christians and atheist,…). Neutral attributes, on the other hand, are denoted by \(W_1, W_2\)
and represent two different stereotypes whose demographic association we are interested in.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}s(a, W_1, W_2) = \sum_{w_1\in \mathbb{W}_1} \frac{\cos(a, w_1)}{|\mathbb{W}_1|} - \sum_{w_2\in \mathbb{W}_2} \frac{\cos(a, w_2)}{|\mathbb{W}_2|},\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}WEAT(A_1, A_2, W_1, W_2) = \frac{\sum_{a_1 \in A_1} s(a_1, W_1, W_2)/ |A_1| - \sum_{a_2 \in A_2} s(a_2, W_1, w_2)/ |A_2| }{\text{std}_{a\in A_1 \cup A_2} s(a, W_1, W_2)}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\section{Probability Metrics}
\label{\detokenize{metrics:probability-metrics}}

\subsection{LPBS}
\label{\detokenize{metrics:lpbs}}\label{\detokenize{metrics:metric-lpbs}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LPBS \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.07337}{(Kurita et al., 2019)} measures bias for a binary demographic group.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\text{LPBS} = \log\frac{p_1}{p_{prior, 1}} - \log\frac{p_2}{p_{prior, 2}}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsection{CBS}
\label{\detokenize{metrics:cbs}}\label{\detokenize{metrics:metric-cbs}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
CBS \sphinxhref{https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.42/}{(Ahn et al., 2021)} generalizes measurement of bias for non\sphinxhyphen{}binary demographic groups.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\text{CBS} =  \text{Var}_{a\in \mathbb{A}}\log\frac{p_a}{p_{prior, a}}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}

Computes CBS score for a list of tuples of dimension n of target words.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{sentences}} (\sphinxhref{https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html\#list}{\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{list}}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{[}}}\sphinxhref{https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html\#str}{\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{str}}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{]}}}) \textendash{} List of sentences with masks

\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {}

\subsection{CPS}
\label{\detokenize{metrics:cps}}\label{\detokenize{metrics:metric-cps}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
CPS \sphinxhref{https://aclanthology.org/2020.emnlp-main.154/}{(Nangia et al., 2020)} uses sentence pairs which coincide in a series of unmodified tokens.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\text{CPS}(S) = \sum_{u\in U} \log \mathbb{P}(u| U_{\backslash u}, A),\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{model}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{nn.Module}}) \textendash{} Language model used to compute probabilities.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{sentences}} (\sphinxhref{https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html\#list}{\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{list}}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{[}}}\sphinxhref{https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html\#str}{\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{str}}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{]}}}) \textendash{} List of sentences for whom we will compute the CPS score.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\end{itemize}

\subsection{AUL}
\label{\detokenize{metrics:aul}}\label{\detokenize{metrics:metric-aul}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
AUL \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.07496}{(Kaneko et al., 2021)} predicts the probability of all tokens in the sentence without masking.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\text{AUL}(S) = \frac{1}{|S|} \sum_{s\in S} \log \mathbb{P}(s|S).\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsection{Demographic Representation}
\label{\detokenize{metrics:demographic-representation}}\label{\detokenize{metrics:metric-dr}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
DR \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.09110}{(Liang et al., 2022)} is computed as follows:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\text{DR}(a) = \sum_{w_i \in \mathbb{A}}\sum_{\hat{Y} \in \hat{\mathbb{Y}}} C(w_i, \hat{Y}),\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsection{HONEST}
\label{\detokenize{metrics:honest}}\label{\detokenize{metrics:metric-honest}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
HONEST \sphinxhref{https://aclanthology.org/2021.naacl-main.191/}{(Nozza et al., 2021)} measures how many of the top \(k\) completions contain harmful words.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\text{HONEST}(\hat{\mathbb{Y}} ) = \frac{\sum_{\hat{Y}_k \in\hat{\mathbb{Y}}_k} \sum_{\hat{y} \in \hat{Y}_k} \mathbf{1}(\hat{y} \in \mathbb{Y}_{hurt} ) }{|\mathbb{\hat{Y}}| k}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\chapter{Algorithms}
\label{\detokenize{algorithms:algorithms}}\label{\detokenize{algorithms::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
FairLangProc provides a comprehensive suite of bias mitigation processors for Large Language Models.


\section{Supported processors}
\label{\detokenize{algorithms:supported-processors}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Fairness processors can be classified according to their stage in the Machine Learning pipeline:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Pre\sphinxhyphen{}processors}: Fairness processors that modify the model inputs (data augmentation, embedding projection,…).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{In\sphinxhyphen{}processors}: Fairness processors that modify the training process (regularizers, adapters,…).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Intra\sphinxhyphen{}processors}: Fairness processors that modify the model’s behavior without further training (attention scaling,…).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The supported methods are:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{algorithms_preprocessors:cda}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Counterfactual Data Augmentation (CDA)}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.06032}{(Webster et al. 2020)}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{algorithms_preprocessors:emb}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Projection based debiasing}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.06520}{(Bolukbasi et al., 2023)}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{algorithms_preprocessors:blind}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Bias removaL wIth No Demographics (BLIND)}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://aclanthology.org/2023.acl-long.490/}{(Orgad et al., 2023)}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{algorithms_inprocessors:adele}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Adapter\sphinxhyphen{}based DEbiasing of LanguagE models (ADELE)}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.03646}{(Lauscher et al., 2021)}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{algorithms_intraprocessors:diff}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Modular Debiasing with Diff Subnetworks}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://aclanthology.org/2023.findings-acl.386/}{(Hauzenberger et al., 2023)}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{algorithms_intraprocessors:eat}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Entropy Attention Temperature (EAT) scaling}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13088}{(Zayed et al., 2023)}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{algorithms_inprocessors:ear}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Entropy Attention Regularizer (EAR)}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.09192}{(Attanasio et al., 2022)}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{algorithms_inprocessors:embreg}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Embedding based regularizer}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10486}{(Liu et al., 2020)}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{algorithms_inprocessors:selective}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Selective unfreezing}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://aclanthology.org/2022.ltedi-1.8/}{(Gira et al., 2024)}.

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Different algorithms have different trade\sphinxhyphen{}offs. See our tutorials for more
detailed comparisons of fairness\sphinxhyphen{}accuracy tradeoffs.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Pre\sphinxhyphen{}processing}
\label{\detokenize{algorithms_preprocessors:pre-processing}}\label{\detokenize{algorithms_preprocessors::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pre\sphinxhyphen{}processors are fairness processors that modify the model inputs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The supported methods are:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{algorithms_preprocessors:cda}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Counterfactual Data Augmentation (CDA)}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.06032}{(Webster et al. 2020)}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{algorithms_preprocessors:emb}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Projection based debiasing}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.06520}{(Bolukbasi et al., 2023)}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{algorithms_preprocessors:blind}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Bias removaL wIth No Demographics (BLIND)}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://aclanthology.org/2023.acl-long.490/}{(Orgad et al., 2023)}.

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Counterfactual Data Augmentation (CDA)}
\label{\detokenize{algorithms_preprocessors:counterfactual-data-augmentation-cda}}\label{\detokenize{algorithms_preprocessors:cda}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Data augmentation is the process of curating or upsampling the dataset to obtain a more representative distribution to train the model on.
In particular, Counterfactual Data Augmentation (CDA) \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.06032}{(Webster et al. 2020)} consists of flipping words with demographic information
while preserving semantic correctness. This procedure can be one\sphinxhyphen{}sided and discard the original sentence or two\sphinxhyphen{}sided to consider both the original and its
augmented version.

\pysigstopsignatures

\subsubsection{Projection\sphinxhyphen{}based debiasing}
\label{\detokenize{algorithms_preprocessors:projection-based-debiasing}}\label{\detokenize{algorithms_preprocessors:emb}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Projection\sphinxhyphen{}based debiasing methods \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.06520}{(Bolukbasi et al., 2023)} operate on latent space, looking to identify a bias subspace given by an
orthogonal basis, \(\{v_i\}_{i=1}^{n_{bias}}\). Then, the hidden representation of any input can be debiased by removing its projection onto this space, formally
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}h_{proj} = h - \sum_{i = 1}^{n_{bias} } \langle h, v_i \rangle \, v_i.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This can be done either at the word or sentence level. In either case the bias subspace is generally identified through PCA,
and usually its dimension is one, resulting in the construction of a bias direction.


\subsubsection{BLIND debiasing}
\label{\detokenize{algorithms_preprocessors:blind-debiasing}}\label{\detokenize{algorithms_preprocessors:blind}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
BLIND \sphinxhref{https://aclanthology.org/2023.acl-long.490/}{(Orgad et al., 2023)} is a debiasing procedure based on a complementary classifier
\(g_{B} : \mathbb{R}^{d_L} \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}\) with parameters \(\theta_{B}\), that takes the hidden representation vector
as inputs and outputs the success probability of the model head for the downstream task. This probability is then used as a weight for said observation
whose magnitude is controlled through a hyper\sphinxhyphen{}parameter \(\gamma \geq 0\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{BLIND} = \left(1 - \sigma \left( g_{B}(h; \theta_{B} ) \right) \right)^{\gamma} \mathcal{L}^{task}(\hat{y}, y).\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The term \(\sigma(g_{B}(h;\theta_B))\) represents the model success probability for the downstream task:
the bigger it is the less weight the observation has, while the smaller it is the more weight it carries.
This forces the model to pay special attention to observations with low probability of success during training.
Note that when \(\gamma = 0\) the original loss function is restored, while \(\gamma >> 1\) exacerbates the effect of the reweighting.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{In\sphinxhyphen{}processing}
\label{\detokenize{algorithms_inprocessors:in-processing}}\label{\detokenize{algorithms_inprocessors::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In\sphinxhyphen{}processors are fairness processors that modify the training process.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The supported methods are:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{algorithms_inprocessors:adele}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Adapter\sphinxhyphen{}based DEbiasing of LanguagE models (ADELE)}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.03646}{(Lauscher et al., 2021)}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{algorithms_inprocessors:ear}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Entropy Attention Regularizer (EAR)}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.09192}{(Attanasio et al., 2022)}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{algorithms_inprocessors:embreg}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Embedding based regularizer}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10486}{(Liu et al., 2020)}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{algorithms_inprocessors:selective}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Selective unfreezing}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://aclanthology.org/2022.ltedi-1.8/}{(Gira et al., 2024)}.

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{ADELE}
\label{\detokenize{algorithms_inprocessors:adele}}\label{\detokenize{algorithms_inprocessors:id1}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The ADELE procedure \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.03646}{(Lauscher et al., 2021)} is based on the adapter framework.
A single adapter module is included to each transformer layer after the feed\sphinxhyphen{}forward sub\sphinxhyphen{}layer, where the outputs are compressed to a bottleneck dimension
\(m\) and then decompressed back to the hidden size of the transformer, \(d_L\). The adapter module itself consists of a two\sphinxhyphen{}layer feed\sphinxhyphen{}forward network:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\text{Adapter}(\mathbf{h}, \mathbf{r}) = U \cdot g(D\cdot \mathbf{h) + \mathbf{r}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\mathbf{h}\) and \(\mathbf{r}\) are the hidden state and residual of the corresponding transformer layer, \(g\) is an activation function and
\(D \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d_L}, U \in \mathbb{R}^{d_L\times m}\) represent the projection matrices.
The idea behind the adapter layer is to introduce an information bottleneck which compresses the latent representation of the inputs,
forcing the model to discard all irrelevant information.

\subsubsection{Embedding based regularizer}
\label{\detokenize{algorithms_inprocessors:embedding-based-regularizer}}\label{\detokenize{algorithms_inprocessors:embreg}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Embedding based regularizers \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10486}{(Liu et al., 2020)} are based on the distance between the embeddings of counterfactual pairs given by \$A\$,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathcal{R} = \sum_{(a_i, a_j)\in A} || M(a_i) - M(a_j)||_2 .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{EAR}
\label{\detokenize{algorithms_inprocessors:ear}}\label{\detokenize{algorithms_inprocessors:id4}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
EAR \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.09192}{(Attanasio et al., 2022)} tries to maximize the entropy of the attention weights to encourage attention to the broader context
of the input,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathcal{R} = - \sum_{l=1}^L \text{entropy}_l(\mathbf{A})\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\text{entropy}_l(\cdot)\) denotes the entropy of the l\sphinxhyphen{}th layer.

\pysigstartsignatures

\subsubsection{Selective unfreezing}
\label{\detokenize{algorithms_inprocessors:selective-unfreezing}}\label{\detokenize{algorithms_inprocessors:selective}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Selective unfreezing \sphinxhref{https://aclanthology.org/2022.ltedi-1.8/}{(Gira et al., 2024)} aims to circumvent catastrophic forgetting during fine\sphinxhyphen{}tuning
by freezing a big amount of the model parameters, which also helps lessening computational expenses.

\subsection{Intra\sphinxhyphen{}processing}
\label{\detokenize{algorithms_intraprocessors:intra-processing}}\label{\detokenize{algorithms_intraprocessors::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Intra\sphinxhyphen{}processors are fairness processors that modify the model’s behavior without further training.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The supported methods are:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{algorithms_intraprocessors:diff}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Modular Debiasing with Diff Subnetworks}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://aclanthology.org/2023.findings-acl.386/}{(Hauzenberger et al., 2023)}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{algorithms_intraprocessors:eat}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Entropy Attention Temperature (EAT) scaling}}}}} \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13088}{(Zayed et al., 2023)}.

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{MoDDiffy}
\label{\detokenize{algorithms_intraprocessors:moddiffy}}\label{\detokenize{algorithms_intraprocessors:diff}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
MoDDiffy \sphinxhref{https://aclanthology.org/2023.findings-acl.386/}{(Hauzenberger et al., 2023)} creates many sparse subnetworks to address bias for different attributes
(gender, religion,…) through the idea of \sphinxstyleemphasis{Diff} prunning. Basically, they freeze the model parameters, \(\theta\),
and train another network with parameters, \(\delta\), with a loss function that promotes accuracy, sparsity and debiasing:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_\rho = \mathcal{L}^{task}_{\rho} + \lambda_{\rho}^0 \mathcal{L}^{0}_{\rho} + \lambda_{\rho}^{debias} \mathcal{L}_{\rho}^{debias},\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{where:}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\mathcal{L}_{\rho}^{task}\) represents the original loss of the downstream task with the new parameters.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\mathcal{L}_{\rho}^{0}\) promotes sparsity through a smooth approximation to the \(L_0\) norm of the new parameters by means of the hard\sphinxhyphen{}concrete distribution of parameters \((\log \alpha_{\rho}, 1)\) and hyper\sphinxhyphen{}parameters \(\gamma < 0, \zeta > 1\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\mathcal{L}_{\rho}^{debias}\) debiases the outputs by approximating the mutual information of embeddings belonging to different demographic groups.

\end{itemize}

\end{description}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In particular the sparsity loss takes the form:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\rho}^{0} = \sum_{i=1}^{|\delta_{\rho}|} \sigma\left( \log \alpha_{\rho, i} - \log\left(- \frac{\gamma}{\zeta}\right) \right).\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
And the debiasing loss:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\rho}^{debias} = \left(\frac{\sum_{x_A \in X^A_\rho} \phi (M(x_A))}{|X_{\rho}^A |} - \frac{\sum_{x_B \in X^B_\rho} \phi (M(x_B))}{|X_{\rho}^B|} \right)^2,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\phi\) is a transformation kernel.

\subsubsection{EAT}
\label{\detokenize{algorithms_intraprocessors:eat}}\label{\detokenize{algorithms_intraprocessors:id2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
EAT scaling \sphinxhref{https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13088}{(Zayed et al., 2023)} modifies the distribution of the attention scores with a temperature\sphinxhyphen{}related parameter,
\(\beta \in [0, \infty)\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\text{Attention}_{\beta} (\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V}) = \text{softmax} \left(\frac{\beta \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{K}}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right) \mathbf{V},\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
the idea being that when \(\beta >> 1\) the head attends only to the tokens with biggest scores while \(\beta \approx 0\) forces the head to attend equally to all tokens.
When \(\beta = 1\) the attention head remains unmodified.

\pysigstartsignatures

\section{Requirements}
\label{\detokenize{tutorials:requirements}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To run the notebooks locally, you need to install FairLangProc and download the datasets:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
pip\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }FairLangProc
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Some notebooks require significant computational resources (GPU recommended).
For GPU acceleration, ensure CUDA is installed and configured.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Verify CUDA availability}
python\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}c\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}import torch; print(f\PYGZsq{}CUDA available: \PYGZob{}torch.cuda.is\PYGZus{}available()\PYGZcb{}\PYGZsq{})\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\end{sphinxadmonition}
